lines.text: I love your verses with all my heart, dear Miss Barrett,--and this is no off-hand complimentary letter that I shall write,--whatever else, no prompt matter-of-course recognition of your genius, and there a graceful and natural end of the thing.
lines.note: Robert's first letter openly declares love for Elizabeth's verses and for her, establishing the courtship.

lines.text: I feel that if I could get myself remade, as if turned to gold, I WOULD not even then desire to become more than the mere setting to that diamond you must always wear.
lines.note: Robert tells Elizabeth she is the diamond and he only the setting, a vivid image of devotion.

lines.text: The tear-marks went away in the moisture of new, happy tears.
lines.note: Elizabeth's tear-marks turning into happy tears shows the emotional turn of their relationship.

lines.text: When I wrote that letter to let you come the first time, do you know, the tears ran down my cheeks....
lines.note: Elizabeth recalls crying when she first allowed Robert to visit, marking how much that first meeting mattered.

lines.text: And now I will dare ... yes, dearest, kiss you back to my heart again; my own.
lines.note: Robert's intimate closing line captures their deepening physical and emotional closeness.

lines.text: I feel, after reading these letters,--as ordinarily after seeing you, sweetest, or hearing from you,--that if marriage did not exist, I should infallibly invent it.
lines.note: Robert's playful declaration that he would invent marriage if it did not exist signals their commitment.

lines.text: My only good in this world--that against which all the world goes for nothing--is to spend my life with you, and be yours.
lines.note: Robert frames his whole good in life as spending it with Elizabeth, anchoring the marriage plan.

lines.text: Can it be the same 'Luria,' I think, that 'golden-hearted Luria,' whom you talked of to me, when you complained of keeping 'wild company,' in the old dear letter?
lines.note: Elizabeth connects the printed 'Luria' back to Robert's earlier 'golden-hearted Luria,' a callback to their literary courtship.

lines.text: ‘know I now what love is!’—Do you remember that the first word I ever wrote to you was ‘I love you, dear Miss Barrett?’
lines.note: Robert recalls that his first written words to Elizabeth were love, echoing the opening of their correspondence.

lines.text: By to-morrow at this time, I shall have you only, to love me—my beloved!
lines.note: Elizabeth's final note imagines having Robert alone to love, closing the poem on their imminent union.
